subject: pharmacology
title: Receptors and pharmacodynamics: the core ideas

steps.tx: Pharmacodynamics studies what a drug does to the body, including its **mechanism of action**. Pharmacokinetics studies what the body does to the drug, covering absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. Keep these two branches separate in your answers. Most receptor questions in NEET-PG and INI-CET test the pharmacodynamic side, so classify each question first.

steps.tx: In G-protein signalling, the **alpha subunit** decides the direction of the response. Gs and Gq are stimulatory, while Gi is inhibitory. Beta receptors work through Gs and raise cAMP. Alpha 2 receptors work through Gi and lower adenylyl cyclase activity. Alpha 1 receptors use Gq, which releases IP3 and DAG, and calcium acts as a **third messenger**.

steps.tx: Drugs can act as **agonists**, which activate the receptor, or as **antagonists**, which block it. A **competitive antagonist** binds the same site as the agonist and shifts the dose-response curve to the right. Its effect can be overcome by more agonist. A **non-competitive antagonist** binds elsewhere, lowers Vmax, and flattens the curve. A partial agonist has high affinity but low intrinsic activity.

steps.tx: Use the dose-response curve to judge a drug. **Potency** is the position on the log curve, and a leftward shift means a lower dose is needed. **Efficacy** is the height, meaning the maximum response. **ED50** is the dose producing half the maximal effect. The **therapeutic index** equals LD50 divided by ED50, and a higher value means a safer drug. Lithium, digoxin and phenytoin have narrow indices.

vis.caption: Log dose-response: competitive antagonist shifts curve right (higher EC50, same Emax); non-competitive depresses Emax.

steps.tx: Remember the physiological antagonists. Adrenaline opposes histamine in bronchial smooth muscle, because it acts on beta 2 receptors while histamine acts on H1 receptors. This is **physiological antagonism**, where two drugs act on different receptors. Heparin and protamine are an example of **chemical antagonism**. Steroid hormones cross the membrane and bind **cytoplasmic or nuclear receptors**, not surface receptors. Insulin uses a tyrosine kinase receptor.
